story.title: Jury in Lindsay Clancy Trial Continues Deliberations Amid Deadlock
story.summary: The jury in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial has entered its fifth day of deliberations after informing the judge that they could not reach a unanimous verdict. The deadlock was reported on Tuesday, prompting the judge to encourage the jurors to keep working towards a decision. If a verdict is not reached, the judge may consider alternative instructions for the jury.

event_overview.title: About Lindsay Clancy Trial
event_overview.subject: Lindsay Clancy Trial
event_overview.summary: The Lindsay Clancy trial is a Massachusetts criminal proceeding over the deaths of Clancy’s three children at the family’s home in Duxbury in January 2023. The central legal question is whether the prosecution can prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible for the alleged killings, after she raised lack of criminal responsibility in connection with postpartum mental illness.

facts.label: Underlying incident
facts.value: Authorities say Duxbury police responded on January 24, 2023, and found three children—Cora, Dawson and Callan Clancy—who later died; the deaths were investigated by Duxbury Police and the Massachusetts State Police Detective Unit assigned to the Plymouth County District Attorney’s Office.

facts.label: Charges and pleas
facts.value: A Plymouth County grand jury indicted Clancy on September 15, 2023, on three murder counts and three strangulation counts. At her October 26, 2023 Superior Court arraignment, she pleaded not guilty; ahead of trial, prosecutors dropped the three strangulation charges, leaving three murder counts for trial.

facts.label: Court and trial status
facts.value: The case is being tried in Plymouth County Superior Court in Massachusetts. As of August 31, 2026, a jury was deliberating after a five-week trial.

facts.label: Legal standard at issue
facts.value: Under Massachusetts’s lack-of-criminal-responsibility standard, once the issue is raised, the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant did not lack substantial capacity, because of mental disease or defect, either to appreciate the wrongfulness or criminality of the conduct or to conform conduct to the law.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows late-July through August 31, 2026 trial developments, especially the competing postpartum-psychosis evidence, mistrial request and jury deliberations; it does not attempt to reproduce the full investigation, pretrial record or all testimony.

explore_lenses.label: What is the jury actually deciding?
explore_lenses.title: Criminal responsibility, not who caused the deaths
explore_lenses.summary: Clancy has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, so the central dispute is whether mental illness rendered her legally not responsible when the children were killed. The jury may consider murder or manslaughter if it finds criminal responsibility, rather than treating the case as a dispute over whether the deaths occurred.

claims.text: Clancy does not deny strangling her three children; she contends that postpartum psychosis led to her actions, while prosecutors argue that she knew what she was doing.

Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague argued that Clancy made a deliberate choice, while defense lawyer Kevin Reddington argued that she was suffering from a disease after a collapse in her mental health and unsuccessful efforts to obtain help.

If jurors find Clancy criminally responsible, they can convict her of murder or manslaughter; an acquittal based on lack of criminal responsibility could still be followed by mental-health confinement if a court finds she presents a public danger.

explore_lenses.label: Why has the case reached a deadlock?
explore_lenses.title: Experts and the parties offered competing accounts
explore_lenses.summary: The trial produced agreement that Clancy had mental-health problems, but sharp conflict over their severity and legal effect at the time of the killings. That makes the deliberations turn on competing interpretations of medical evidence, treatment records, and her conduct.

claims.text: Relatives and clinicians testified about a decline in Clancy's mental health, including treatment with multiple medications and a psychiatric-hospital stay, while prosecution and defense experts reached sharply different conclusions about her psychiatric state at the time of the killings.
The prosecution argued that Clancy's failure to tell providers about earlier thoughts of harming her children, and the timing of sending her husband on errands, showed awareness and planning.
The defense argued that Clancy was overmedicated, misdiagnosed, and failed by providers as her condition deteriorated; Reddington also challenged aspects of the police investigation.
The jurors' September 1 note said only that they could not reach a unanimous decision; it did not disclose a vote count or the basis of their disagreement.

explore_lenses.label: What happens if no verdict is reached?
explore_lenses.title: The judge can declare a mistrial; prosecutors choose next steps
explore_lenses.summary: Judge William Sullivan has instructed the jury to continue deliberating rather than immediately ending the case. If the jury ultimately cannot agree, Massachusetts procedure permits a mistrial, after which the prosecution must decide whether and how to proceed.

claims.text: Massachusetts Criminal Procedure Rule 27 provides that a court may declare a mistrial when a jury cannot reach a verdict.
As of September 2, Sullivan had returned jurors to deliberations after their deadlock notice; no mistrial had been declared.
If there is a mistrial, the murder charges remain pending and prosecutors can seek a new trial, dismiss the case, or negotiate a plea resolution.

Forecast: Brad Bailey, a Boston defense attorney and former prosecutor not involved in the case, said a mistrial could prompt prosecutors to consider a plea offer, while the defense would likely press against a retrial.

story_report.summary: Jurors in Lindsay Clancy’s trial continued deliberating for a fifth day after telling the judge Tuesday that they could not reach a unanimous verdict. The judge instructed them to keep working, leaving the case without a verdict because unanimity is required for either conviction or acquittal. The jury has not publicly disclosed what is dividing it. The central question at trial is whether Clancy was criminally responsible when she strangled her three children, an act she does not deny.

sections.heading: Criminal Responsibility Drives Clancy Trial
sections.body: Clancy contends that postpartum psychosis led to her actions, while prosecutors argue that she knew what she was doing. Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said Clancy made a deliberate choice; defense lawyer Kevin Reddington argued that a disease followed a collapse in Clancy’s mental health and unsuccessful efforts to obtain help. Relatives and clinicians described a decline in her mental health, including multiple medications and a psychiatric-hospital stay, but prosecution and defense experts reached sharply different conclusions about her psychiatric state at the time of the killings.

sections.heading: Deadlock Leaves Mistrial Option Open
sections.body: As of Sept. 2, the judge had returned jurors to deliberations and had not declared a mistrial. Under Massachusetts Criminal Procedure Rule 27, a court may declare a mistrial when a jury cannot reach a verdict. If jurors find Clancy criminally responsible, they can convict her of murder or manslaughter; an acquittal based on lack of criminal responsibility could still lead to mental-health confinement if a court finds she presents a public danger. A mistrial would leave the murder charges pending, allowing prosecutors to seek a new trial, dismiss the case or negotiate a plea resolution.

unresolved.text: The jury’s note did not disclose a vote count or identify whether disagreement involves criminal responsibility, the degree of homicide, individual counts, or other evidence.
No fixed publicly reported point requires the judge to declare a mistrial.

related_stories.summary: The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier has arrived in eastern Thailand after more than nine months at sea, primarily spent in the Middle East. Reports have emerged regarding challenging conditions on board, including food shortages and plumbing issues, prompting calls from some lawmakers for an investigation into the deployment's impact on crew welfare.
